mockText: 65 items in 170 minutes, like the real exam, with 4 hands-on items, flags and a review screen. The real SCS-C03 mixes multiple choice and multiple response with ordering and matching items; the hands-on items here practice those skills.
lead: AWS's security deep dive. It proves you can detect threats, respond to incidents, lock down networks and compute, design IAM at scale, protect data with encryption and secrets, and govern many accounts at once. AWS recommends years of hands-on AWS security work, so it fits best after Solutions Architect Associate and some real cloud time.
objSub: Six domains and 16 task statements from AWS's SCS-C03 exam guide. Tick them off as you study; progress saves on this device.

c03.label: C03
c03.note: The only version on sale. It replaced SCS-C02 (last day Dec 1, 2025). C03 splits detection and incident response into their own domains, makes IAM the biggest domain, and adds generative AI guardrails and centralized root access. It also adds ordering and matching questions.
c03.onote: Official AWS task statements (SCS-C03 exam guide), in plain words. Weights are AWS's share of scored content.

domains.name: Detection
obj: Monitoring and alerting for an account or organization

Decide what to watch for each workload; health checks; collect findings in Security Hub; CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards for anomalies; automate regular checks with Config, Inspector and GuardDuty.
Logging solutions

Pick log sources (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 Resolver logs, WAF, load balancer and app logs); store them centrally in S3 or Security Lake; query them with Athena and CloudWatch Logs Insights; normalize and correlate them with OpenSearch.
Troubleshoot monitoring, logging and alerting
Find why logs or alerts are missing: bucket or KMS key policies, a stopped trail, a broken CloudWatch agent config, the wrong Region, or an EventBridge rule that doesn't match.

domains.name: Incident Response
obj: Design and test an incident response plan

Runbooks and playbooks (Systems Manager); limit the blast radius with separate accounts; set up access, tools and a forensic account ahead of time; test with game days and Fault Injection Service; automate fixes with EventBridge and Lambda.
Respond to security events

Capture evidence (snapshots, memory, logs) before you change anything; search and correlate across services; confirm scope and impact with Detective; contain, eradicate and recover; find the root cause.

domains.name: Infrastructure Security
obj: Network edge services

Choose edge protection by threat: AWS WAF rules (managed rule groups, rate limits, geo match, bot control), Shield Advanced for DDoS, CloudFront with origin access control; fit in third-party edge tools.
Compute workloads

Hardened AMIs and container images; the right instance, task and execution roles; Inspector scans; patching with Systems Manager; Session Manager instead of open SSH; security checks in CI/CD pipelines; guardrails for generative AI apps.
Network security controls

Security groups, network ACLs and Network Firewall; secure hybrid and multi-cloud links (VPN, Direct Connect); segment networks by sensitivity; find unneeded access with Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer.

domains.name: Identity and Access Management
obj: Authentication strategies

Identity for people (IAM Identity Center with an external IdP over SAML or OIDC), apps (Cognito) and machines (roles, IAM Roles Anywhere); temporary credentials from STS; troubleshoot failed sign-ins and federation.
Authorization strategies

Identity, resource, session and permissions boundary policies; SCPs and RCPs; RBAC vs ABAC with tags; least privilege with IAM Access Analyzer; read the policy evaluation logic to explain an Access Denied; Verified Permissions for app authorization.

domains.name: Data Protection
obj: Data in transit
Require TLS (the aws:SecureTransport condition, load balancer security policies); private access with VPC endpoints and PrivateLink; encryption between nodes and services.
Data at rest
KMS vs CloudHSM; server-side vs client-side encryption; integrity with S3 Object Lock, versioning and code signing; lifecycle and retention rules; secure backups with AWS Backup against ransomware.
Confidential data, credentials, secrets and key material
Secrets Manager rotation; imported key material and external key stores; customer managed and multi-Region KMS keys; AWS Private CA and ACM; masking with CloudWatch Logs data protection policies.

domains.name: Security Foundations and Governance
obj: Centrally deploy and manage accounts

AWS Organizations and Control Tower controls; SCPs, RCPs, AI opt-out and declarative policies; delegated administrator accounts for security services; centralized root access, root MFA and break-glass plans.
Secure, consistent deployments
Infrastructure as code with CloudFormation StackSets, Guard and cfn-lint; a tagging strategy; central policy with Firewall Manager; safe sharing with Service Catalog and AWS RAM.
Evaluate compliance
Config rules with automatic remediation; Security Hub standards; evidence with Audit Manager and AWS Artifact; Well-Architected Tool reviews against the Security Pillar.

extras.title: Who does what
rows: Finds threats in CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs and more
Scans EC2, container images and Lambda for known CVEs
Finds sensitive data, like PII, in S3
Collects findings and checks accounts against standards
Graphs activity so you can scope an incident
Records resource settings over time; rules flag drift
Who called which API, when and from where
Central security logs from many accounts, in one format (OCSF)

extras.title: Policy types
rows: Max permissions for accounts in an OU. Grants nothing
Max permissions on resources, like S3 and KMS, in the org
Attached to a user, group or role
On the resource itself; can allow other accounts
The most a user or role can ever get

extras.title: How AWS decides
rows: An explicit Deny in any policy wins. Stop.
An SCP or RCP that doesn't allow the action blocks it.
A resource policy can allow it (enough on its own for a same-account IAM user).
Otherwise an identity policy must allow it.
A permissions boundary, if there is one, must also allow it.
A session policy, if there is one, must also allow it. Nothing allowed it? Implicit deny.

extras.title: Compromised EC2 instance
rows: Don't terminate it. Turn on termination protection and tag it.
Isolate it with a security group that allows nothing (add a NACL rule to cut connections already open).
Take it out of its Auto Scaling group and load balancer.
Snapshot its EBS volumes, and capture memory if you can.
Revoke the instance role's active sessions.
Investigate from a separate forensic account with Detective and the logs.
Rebuild from a known-good image, then fix the root cause.

method: Use the six domains above. IAM is the biggest at 20%, and policy questions show up everywhere.
One C03 course, then read the AWS Security Incident Response Guide and the policy evaluation logic page. Avoid C02-only material.
In a personal account: an organization with an SCP, a CloudTrail org trail to an encrypted bucket, GuardDuty and Security Hub with a delegated admin, a KMS key policy you break and fix.
Practice on legal targets made for it: flaws.cloud, and CloudGoat in your own account. Never test accounts you don't own.
Timed practice exams labeled SCS-C03. For every miss, write which policy or setting made the difference.
tips: When a question shows JSON, check Effect, Action, Resource and Condition in that order. One word, like a missing service principal, is usually the answer.
In incident questions, capture and isolate before you stop, delete or patch. Answers that destroy evidence are wrong.
If the question says “ensure” or “prevent,” look for an SCP, RCP or policy. Config and GuardDuty only tell you after it happens.
170 minutes is about 2.5 minutes a question. Long JSON questions deserve it; flag and move on from the rest.

quiz.q: An organization trail sends logs to a central S3 bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Right after someone edited the key policy, new log files stopped arriving. What's the MOST likely cause?
o: The key policy no longer lets the CloudTrail service principal use the key to encrypt (kms:GenerateDataKey*)
Right. CloudTrail needs permission in the key policy to generate data keys. Without it, delivery fails.
S3 Block Public Access was turned on
Block Public Access stops public access. CloudTrail writes as a service through the bucket policy, which isn't public.
GuardDuty was turned off
GuardDuty reads CloudTrail events. It has nothing to do with delivering log files.
The trail only logs the home Region
A single-Region trail would still deliver that Region's logs. Nothing would stop entirely.

quiz.q: Security wants an alert within minutes whenever anyone uses the root user in any account in the organization. What works BEST?
o: Send the organization trail to CloudWatch Logs, add a metric filter for root activity, and alarm to an SNS topic
Right. Every account's root activity lands in one log group, and the alarm fires within minutes.
Review the IAM credential report every week
Weekly isn't within minutes.
Turn on the AWS Config rule that checks root MFA
That rule checks whether MFA is on. It doesn't alert when root is used.
Check Trusted Advisor's root account check
Trusted Advisor looks at settings, like root MFA, not live activity.

quiz.q: GuardDuty reports an IAM user's access key making API calls from a known malicious IP address. What should you do FIRST?
o: Deactivate the access key, then review what it did in CloudTrail
Right. Deactivating stops the attacker now, and keeps the key and the user so you can investigate.
Delete the IAM user
It stops the attack, but you lose the user's policies and history you need for the investigation.
Archive the GuardDuty finding
Archiving hides the alert. The attacker keeps going.
Require MFA for the user's console sign-in
Console MFA doesn't stop API calls made with an access key.

quiz.q: Your playbook for a compromised EC2 instance must keep all evidence. What should happen BEFORE the instance is stopped?
o: Capture memory and snapshot the EBS volumes
Right. Memory is lost when the instance stops, and snapshots preserve the disks as they were.
Run antivirus and delete the malware
That changes the evidence. Clean up only after you've captured it.
Patch and reboot the instance
A reboot wipes memory, and patching changes the disk.
Change it to a smaller instance type
Changing the type requires a stop and doesn't help the investigation.

quiz.q: A login page behind CloudFront gets credential-stuffing bursts from thousands of IP addresses, each sending about 200 requests in 5 minutes. Real users send a few. What blocks the abuse with the least effort?
o: An AWS WAF rate-based rule scoped to the login path
Right. Rate-based rules block any IP that goes over the limit for that path, however many IPs there are.
Network ACL deny rules for each IP
NACLs have a small rule limit and can't keep up with thousands of changing IPs. They also don't apply at CloudFront.
Shield Advanced on its own
Shield Advanced targets DDoS. Credential stuffing needs WAF rules.
Security group deny rules
Security groups can't deny. They only have allow rules.

quiz.q: Auditors want no inbound SSH on any instance, and every admin session logged. What meets both?
o: Systems Manager Session Manager with session logging to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, and port 22 closed
Right. Session Manager needs no inbound ports and can log every session.
A bastion host with SSH logging
The bastion still accepts inbound SSH.
EC2 Instance Connect
It still uses SSH on port 22, and it doesn't log what admins type.
A VPN, then SSH to each instance
SSH is still open inbound, just from the VPN.

quiz.q: Instances in a VPC may reach the internet only for an approved list of domain names, like updates.example.com. Which control enforces this?
o: AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule
Right. Network Firewall can allow outbound traffic by domain name.
Security groups
Security groups filter by IP address and port, not domain names.
Network ACLs
NACLs are stateless and filter by IP address only.
AWS WAF
WAF protects inbound web requests to CloudFront, load balancers and API Gateway, not outbound traffic.

quiz.q: A developer's role has this identity policy. Their account's SCP was changed to allow ONLY ec2:* and s3:Get*. What happens when they call s3:PutObject on reports-bucket?
o: Denied, because the SCP doesn't allow PutObject
Right. An SCP sets the maximum. If it doesn't allow an action, no identity policy can.
Allowed, because the identity policy allows s3:*
The identity policy allows it, but the SCP caps what anyone in the account can do.
Allowed, because SCPs only apply to the root user
SCPs apply to every user and role in member accounts, root included.
Denied, because identity policies can't use wildcards
Wildcards like s3:* are allowed in policies.

quiz.q: Five hundred project teams each have a role. Each role should manage only EC2 instances tagged with its own project. Which approach needs the LEAST policy work as teams are added?
o: One policy whose condition matches aws:ResourceTag/project to aws:PrincipalTag/project
Right. That's attribute-based access control (ABAC). New teams just need tags.
One policy per team that lists its instance IDs
You'd edit a policy every time an instance is launched.
One IAM group per team with its own policy
That's role-based access. It means 500 policies to maintain.
One SCP per team
SCPs apply to accounts, not to teams inside an account, and they don't grant access.

quiz.q: The unit uses Microsoft Entra ID and has 40 AWS accounts. People must sign in once with their existing credentials and get the right role in each account, with no IAM users. What should you set up?
o: IAM Identity Center with Entra ID as the external identity provider, and permission sets assigned to accounts
Right. Single sign-on, automatic user sync, and one place to manage access to all 40 accounts.
An IAM user in each account with the same password
That's 40 sets of long-lived credentials, which the requirement rules out.
An Amazon Cognito user pool
Cognito is for app users, not staff signing in to AWS accounts.
IAM Roles Anywhere
Roles Anywhere gives workloads outside AWS temporary credentials using certificates. It isn't for people.

quiz.q: A contract requires single-tenant HSMs that only the unit's own crypto officers control. Which service fits?
o: AWS CloudHSM
Right. CloudHSM gives you dedicated HSMs in your VPC, and you manage the users and keys.
AWS KMS with a customer managed key
KMS uses HSMs that AWS runs as a shared, multi-tenant service.
AWS KMS with imported key material
You supply the key material, but it still lives in KMS's shared service.
S3 server-side encryption with S3 managed keys
AWS manages those keys entirely.

quiz.q: A bucket policy must reject any request that doesn't use HTTPS. Which statement does that?
o: A Deny for all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false
Right. An explicit Deny blocks plain HTTP no matter what any other policy allows.
An Allow for all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is true
Other policies could still allow HTTP. Only a Deny guarantees the block.
Default encryption with SSE-KMS
That protects data at rest, not in transit.
S3 Block Public Access
That stops public access. It doesn't require HTTPS.

quiz.q: The security team wants to run GuardDuty for all 60 accounts from a security tooling account, not the management account, and turn it on for new accounts automatically. What should they do?
o: Make the security account GuardDuty's delegated administrator and turn on auto-enable
Right. One account sees every finding and new accounts are covered on their own.
Sign in to each account and turn GuardDuty on
It's slow, leaves findings in 60 places, and misses new accounts.
Run GuardDuty from the management account
AWS advises keeping daily security work out of the management account.
Deploy GuardDuty with StackSets only
It can turn it on, but you still lack one central view of findings.

quiz.q: Any S3 bucket that becomes public must be found and fixed automatically, with a history that proves compliance over time. What fits BEST?
o: An AWS Config rule for public buckets with automatic remediation through Systems Manager Automation
Right. Config finds it, fixes it and keeps the compliance history.
CloudTrail alone
CloudTrail records the change, but it doesn't judge or fix anything.
A weekly Trusted Advisor review
Not automatic, and too slow.
Amazon Macie
Macie finds sensitive data. It isn't built to fix bucket settings.

quiz.q: Leadership wants member accounts to have no root passwords or root MFA devices to manage, but still be able to do root-only tasks, like removing a bucket policy that locks everyone out. What should you use?
o: Centralized root access in IAM, using privileged root sessions from the management or delegated admin account
Right. Root credentials are removed from member accounts, and short root sessions handle the rare root-only tasks.
Keep each root password and MFA device in a safe
It works, but it's exactly the credential management they want to get rid of.
An SCP that denies everything to root
Then nobody could do root-only tasks when needed.
Delete the root user in each member account
You can't delete an account's root user.

pbqs.title: Which service caught it?
pbqs.scenario: Six findings came in this week. Pick the AWS service that reports each one. Each answer is used once; three are distractors.

items.text: An EC2 instance is talking to a known crypto-mining pool.
items.why: GuardDuty spots threats in network, DNS and API activity.

items.text: A container image in ECR has a critical OpenSSL vulnerability.
items.why: Inspector scans images, instances and Lambda functions for known CVEs.

items.text: A bucket holds spreadsheets full of Social Security numbers.
items.why: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

items.text: You need every IP address and role tied to an alert over the past month to scope it.
items.why: Detective graphs related activity so you can see an incident's scope.

items.text: A KMS key policy lets an account outside your organization use the key.
items.why: IAM Access Analyzer flags resources shared outside your zone of trust.

items.text: A bucket's settings drifted from the required configuration last Tuesday.
items.why: Config records settings over time and its rules flag drift.

pbqs.title: Contain the incident
pbqs.scenario: Five incidents are open. Pick the containment step that stops each one fastest while keeping evidence. Each step is used once; two are distractors.

rows.req: An IAM user's access key was pushed to a public GitHub repo.
rows.why: Deactivating the key stops its use at once and keeps it for the investigation.

rows.req: An attacker stole temporary credentials from an EC2 instance's role.
rows.why: Revoking active sessions denies every token issued before now, even ones not expired.

rows.req: An instance is beaconing to a command-and-control server. You need it for forensics.
rows.why: A security group that allows nothing cuts it off without destroying evidence.

rows.req: A database password turned up in a public paste.
rows.why: Rotate it in Secrets Manager so the leaked password stops working.

rows.req: One IP address is hammering the login page through CloudFront.
rows.why: A WAF IP set rule blocks it at the edge.

pbqs.title: Allowed or denied?
pbqs.scenario: For each request, decide what AWS's policy evaluation returns. All in one account; the SCP allows everything unless stated.

rows.req: A role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on the bucket. Nothing else applies.
rows.why: An identity policy allows it and nothing denies it.

rows.req: A role's identity policy allows s3:*, but the bucket policy has a Deny for that role.
rows.why: An explicit Deny anywhere wins over every Allow.

rows.req: No policy says anything about the action.
rows.why: Everything is denied unless something allows it.

rows.req: Identity policy allows ec2:*. The role's permissions boundary allows only s3:*. The call is ec2:RunInstances.
rows.why: The boundary doesn't allow EC2, so the request is implicitly denied.

rows.req: The bucket policy allows IAM user Ana s3:GetObject. Ana's identity policies say nothing about S3.
rows.why: In the same account, a resource policy that names the user is enough on its own.

rows.req: Identity policy allows kms:Decrypt, but the key policy doesn't mention the role and doesn't let IAM policies grant access.
rows.why: A KMS key policy must allow access itself, or delegate to IAM. Here it does neither.

mapSub: Security Specialty is the top of the AWS line for cloud security. Tap any cert to jump to it.

keep.text: Recertify by passing the latest Security Specialty exam (your 50% voucher works), or add 1 year with AWS Skill Builder's maintenance option and a paid subscription.
keep.after: Maintenance opens in the last 90 days before it expires. Other AWS exams don't renew a Specialty, and your cert must still be active.

keep.text: AWS recommends 5 years of IT security work and 2 or more years securing AWS workloads. It's a recommendation, not a requirement to sit the exam.
keep.after: The exam guide puts it as 3 to 5 years securing cloud solutions.

keep.text: No AWS cert is on the DoD 8140 matrix (V3.0). For a coded billet, pair it with one that is, like CCSP or CISSP.
keep.after: Defense contractors often ask for both: an 8140 cert for the contract and an AWS cert for the work.

keep.text: Check that CG COOL lists the credential before you request funding.
keep.after: If you passed another AWS exam first, use your 50% discount voucher. After you get out, the VA reimburses AWS exam fees under any GI Bill with an education benefit.
